title: Into Your Hand
sum: Psalm 31 (Psalm 30 in the Greek and Latin numbering) swings back and forth between fear and trust. A man hunted by enemies, worn out by grief and forgotten like a dead man, prays to God as his rock and fortress. Twice he moves from panic to confidence, and he ends by calling everyone who waits for the LORD to stand firm.

Its central line, "Into your hand I place my spirit" (31:5), became the dying prayer of Jesus in Luke and the bedtime prayer of Jews and Christians. Its language overlaps with Jeremiah (31:13) and with Psalm 71, and its structure shows how a lament can turn into praise before the danger is over.
readings: Read as a prayer in danger

The speaker is in real trouble: plots, slander, sickness and isolation (31:9–13). The psalm models how to pray in it: name the danger, hand your life over to God, remember his loyal love, and speak to others about it.
Because Jesus prays 31:5 on the cross (Luke 23:46), Christian readers hear the whole psalm in his voice: abandoned by friends (31:11), plotted against (31:13), trusting the Father to the end.

views.H: The title gives no occasion. Readers who take David as author link the besieged city of 31:21 to Keilah, where Saul tried to trap him (1 Samuel 23:7–13), and the panic of 31:22 to David's flight in the wilderness of Maon (1 Samuel 23:26).
views.C: Scholars classify it as an individual lament with thanksgiving. Its many echoes of Jeremiah and of other psalms (Psalm 71; Jonah 2) lead many to think it was composed from traditional phrases, perhaps late in the monarchy or after it. Some think verses 19–24 were sung after a rescue, at the temple.
views.L: The church prays 31:1–6 at night prayer (Compline), with the responsory In manus tuas, Domine. Its bedtime use matches Jewish practice, where 31:5 is said before sleep.
views.J: The Jewish bedtime Shema includes 31:5, and the last stanza of the hymn Adon Olam, sung at the end of many services, takes it up. Commentators such as Radak read it as David's prayer during his flight from Saul.
views.X: Luke 23:46 puts 31:5 on Jesus' lips with "Father" added; Stephen (Acts 7:59) and later martyrs died with it. Luther and many others prayed it at their deaths.

echoes: Luke 23:46; Acts 7:59; 1 Peter 4:19; Jeremiah 20:10; Jonah 2:4; Jonah 2:8; Psalm 71:1–3; Psalm 18:2; 2 Samuel 22:2–3; Numbers 6:25

settings.what: A prayer for rescue that turns to thanks
settings.to: God (31:1–22), then the faithful who worship with him (31:23–24)
settings.when: under attack by enemies and slander, sick and shunned; the closing verses look back on an answer
settings.why: to put the sufferer's life in God's hand and to give the faithful a pattern for trust when the danger is not yet over; the last two verses turn a private prayer into a public sermon
settings.readers: After the exile, Israelites praying together used it as a prayer of any person in danger. Because the speaker calls others to "stay strong", it was suited to the gathered community.
views: A person accused or in danger comes to the temple to pray and waits for God's answer (Kraus).
The prayer of David hunted by Saul, as tradition reads it.

traditions.q: "Into your hand I place my spirit": where does the spirit go at death?
views: The soul is judged at death and goes to heaven, to purgatory for cleansing, or to hell, and awaits the resurrection of the body (Catechism 1021–1022, 1030).
The soul lives on and has a foretaste of its final state; the church prays for the departed until the resurrection.
The souls of the righteous are at once made perfect and received into heaven, and the souls of the wicked are cast into hell, until the resurrection (Westminster Confession 32.1).
Death is an unconscious sleep. The "spirit" committed to God is the breath of life, which returns to him; the person lives again at the resurrection (Fundamental Beliefs 26).
There is no immortal soul. The spirit is the life-force that returns to God; the dead are unconscious until resurrection.

title: The Relief of Confession
sum: Psalm 32 (Greek 31) begins with a double "Happy": the joy of the person whose sin God has lifted away. Then the poet tells his story. As long as he kept silent his body wasted away under God's heavy hand; when he finally confessed, God forgave. He urges every faithful person to pray while God can be found, and a voice (God's or the poet's) promises to teach the way, so that no one needs to be dragged like a mule.

It is the first psalm called a maskil, one of the church's seven penitential psalms, and the text Paul quotes in Romans 4 for God not counting sin. Possidius says the dying Augustine had the penitential psalms posted on his wall.

views.H: Tradition links it with David's confession after Bathsheba (2 Samuel 12:13), as Psalm 51 is linked by its title. Psalm 32 has no such title.
views.C: A thanksgiving for forgiveness, sung in the temple after recovery, with wisdom teaching (32:8–10). Many see sickness behind 32:3–4. It is often dated to the monarchy, though wisdom features suggest to some a later date.
views.L: The second of the seven penitential psalms in the church, used in Lent and before confession.
views.J: The Talmud (Berakhot 8a) collects rabbis' answers to what "the time for finding you" (32:6) means: finding a wife, the Torah, a peaceful death, a proper burial, and (as a joke with a point) a toilet; all are things to pray for.
views.X: Paul quotes 32:1–2 (Romans 4:6–8) for justification by faith. Possidius says the dying Augustine had the penitential psalms written out and posted on the wall so he could read them, weeping.

deep.b: Paul's argument in Romans 4 joins Genesis 15:6 ("he reckoned it to him as righteousness") with Psalm 32:2 ("the person the LORD does not charge with guilt"), because both use the verb "count, reckon" (chashav, Greek logizomai). A rabbinic way of reading, joining texts by a shared word, lets him say that David speaks of the happiness of the one to whom God counts righteousness apart from works (Romans 4:6). Lutheran and Reformed readers find here forgiveness received by faith alone. Catholic and Orthodox readers agree that forgiveness is God's free gift, and stress that the psalm also includes confession and a changed life (32:5, 32:8–10). Some recent scholars (the "new perspective") read Paul's point as being about Gentiles' inclusion without circumcision.

echoes: Romans 4:6–8; Genesis 15:6; 2 Samuel 12:13; Proverbs 28:13; 1 John 1:9; Isaiah 55:6; Psalm 51:1–4; Psalm 38:1–4

settings.what: A thanksgiving for forgiveness, with teaching
settings.to: the congregation (32:1–2, 32:11), God (32:3–7), and a learner addressed as "you" (32:8–9)
settings.when: after recovery from sin and perhaps sickness; offered at the temple
settings.why: to tell others how confession brought relief, so that they will not hide their sin as he did; the teaching voice turns his story into instruction
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, with the temple rebuilt and confession central to its worship (Ezra 9; Nehemiah 9), the psalm taught that God forgives the one who stops hiding.
views: The promise to teach is God's answer to the forgiven person.
The forgiven poet now instructs others, as a maskil does (Calvin).

traditions.q: Must sins be confessed to a priest?
views: Serious (mortal) sins must be confessed to a priest in the sacrament of penance, at least once a year; the priest absolves in Christ's name (Catechism 1456–1457; Trent).
Confession is made to Christ in the presence of the priest, who is a witness and gives the prayer of absolution; it is expected regularly, especially before communion.
Private confession and absolution are kept and valued, but listing every sin is not required; the absolution is God's own word of forgiveness (Augsburg Confession 11 and 25).
General confession is made in the service; private confession to a priest is offered for those with a troubled conscience, but not required ("all may, none must, some should").
Confession is made to God, and to people one has wronged; there is no sacrament of penance (Westminster Confession 15.5–6).
Each believer confesses directly to God through Christ the one mediator; confession to one another is for mutual help, not absolution.

title: The Word That Made the World
sum: Psalm 33 (Greek 32) is a hymn that answers the end of Psalm 32: "Shout for joy, you righteous!" It calls for a new song with lyre and harp, and gives the reasons: the LORD's word is upright, and by that word he made the heavens and stored up the sea. He breaks the plans of nations, but his own plan stands. Happy is the nation he chose. No king is saved by his army or his horses; the LORD's eye is on those who fear him.
It has 22 verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, though it is not an acrostic. It is the only psalm in Psalms 3–41 besides Psalm 10 with no Hebrew title.

views.H: With no title, tradition is free. The Greek calls it "Of David".
views.C: A hymn of praise for the community, possibly sung at a festival. Its 22 lines, the creation-by-word theme close to Genesis 1, and wisdom features lead many to date it late, after the exile. Others see older hymn forms.
views.L: In the Jewish Sabbath morning service Psalm 33 is one of the extra psalms in the morning praises (Pesukei Dezimra). In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours it is sung at Morning Prayer (Lauds) on Tuesday of Week I.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition reads 33:6 with the ten sayings of creation (Mishnah Avot 5:1) and 33:9 as God creating by speech alone.
views.X: Christians read "word" and "breath" (33:6) with John 1:1–3 and Genesis 1:2: the Son and the Spirit at work in creation (Irenaeus). Hebrews 11:3 says the worlds were framed by God's word.

echoes: Genesis 1:1–31; John 1:1–3; Hebrews 11:3; 2 Peter 3:5; Exodus 15:8; Psalm 20:7; Isaiah 31:1; Deuteronomy 17:16; Revelation 5:9

settings.by: a temple singer or the worshiping community (no title in Hebrew)
settings.to: the righteous gathered for worship (33:1–3), all the earth (33:8), and God (33:22)
settings.when: a festival or regular temple worship; perhaps a victory or a deliverance not depending on military strength (33:16–17)
settings.why: to teach that the creator who made the world by a word also rules history, so his people should trust him rather than armies
settings.readers: For Israel after the exile, without a king or army, the psalm said that the nation's safety lay in the LORD's plan, not in horses.

title: Taste and See
sum: Psalm 34 (Greek 33) is an alphabet poem of thanks and teaching. Its title sets it after David's escape from the king of Gath by pretending to be mad. The first half praises God for rescue and invites the humble to "taste and see" that the LORD is good. The second half becomes a lesson: "Come, children": whoever wants a good life must guard his tongue, turn from evil, and pursue peace.
The New Testament uses it three times: 1 Peter quotes 34:8 and 34:12–16, and John sees 34:20 fulfilled when Jesus' bones are not broken. The early church sang it at communion.

views.H: The title points to 1 Samuel 21:10–15. Readers who trust it note that the poor man who cried out (34:6) is David alone and helpless; the angel encamped (34:7) and the young lions (34:10) suit his wilderness life. The name Abimelech for Achish is explained as a royal title.
views.C: An acrostic thanksgiving with a wisdom lesson. The alphabet form, the teacher's "children" and the closeness to Proverbs lead most to date it after the exile. The title is seen as a scribe's link made through the shared word ta'am (sense, taste: 34:0 and 34:8).
views.L: In Jewish worship Psalm 34 is said on Sabbath mornings, and 34:9–10 is near the end of the grace after meals. In the church it was the communion psalm from the 300s; in the Russian Orthodox use it is read at the end of the Divine Liturgy.
views.J: The Midrash on Psalms tells that David once asked God what use madness was, and learned the answer at Gath when pretending madness saved him. The rabbis turned 34:14 into a rule: peace must be pursued.
views.X: 1 Peter 2:3 and 3:10–12 use the psalm for new Christians facing abuse. John 19:36 reads 34:20 (with the Passover law) at the cross. Cyril of Jerusalem explains 34:8 to the newly baptized as the invitation to communion.

deep.b: Each verse begins with the next letter: 1 alef, 2 bet, 3 gimel, 4 dalet, 5 he, (no waw), 6 zayin, 7 chet, 8 tet, 9 yod, 10 kaf, 11 lamed, 12 mem, 13 nun, 14 samekh, 15 ayin, 16 pe, 17 tsade, 18 qof, 19 resh, 20 shin, 21 tav, and 22 an extra pe. Psalm 25 has the same pattern, missing waw and with a closing pe line. Some think the waw line dropped out; others think the pattern is deliberate, so that the first, middle and last lines (alef, lamed, pe) spell alef, "learn".

echoes: 1 Samuel 21:10–15; 1 Peter 2:3; 1 Peter 3:10–12; John 19:36; Exodus 12:46; Numbers 9:12; Psalm 25:1–22; Proverbs 1:7; Hebrews 1:14

settings.by: the rescued poet (the title: David after Gath)
settings.to: the humble who gather to hear (34:2–3), invited to share his praise
settings.when: after a rescue; the title says after David escaped from the Philistine king by feigning madness
settings.why: to make one person's rescue a reason for others to trust, and to invite them to "taste" God's goodness for themselves
settings.readers: For the community after the exile, the poor (34:6) and humble (34:2) were a name for the faithful, and the psalm promised that God hears them.

settings.by: the poet as a wisdom teacher
settings.to: "children", that is, students or the young (34:11)
settings.when: teaching in the home, the temple courts, or a school of wise men
settings.why: to teach the fear of the LORD as a way of life: honest speech, turning from evil, pursuing peace; and to promise that God keeps the righteous though they suffer
settings.readers: Jewish readers used it to teach ethics of speech; Christians (1 Peter 3:10–12) applied it to believers slandered for their faith.

title: Fight for Me
sum: Psalm 35 (Greek 34) is the prayer of a man surrounded by false accusers. He asks God to take up his lawsuit and to arm himself for battle; he asks that his attackers be shamed, chased by the angel of the LORD and caught in their own nets. In the middle he tells what hurt most: he had fasted and mourned for these men when they were sick, and they laughed when he stumbled.

It is one of the curse psalms, and it is honest about the wish to see enemies ruined. It also hands that wish to God as judge instead of taking revenge. Jesus quotes the line "they hated me without cause" from it or from Psalm 69 (John 15:25).

views.H: Readers who take it as David's think of Saul's court, where David had served loyally and was repaid with hatred (1 Samuel 18–24), or of the time of Absalom.
views.C: An individual lament of an accused person, with three sections that each end in a vow of praise (35:9–10, 35:18, 35:27–28). Some see a king facing treaty-breakers among his allies (the military language); most see a falsely accused worshiper in a temple trial.
views.L: In the Roman Liturgy of the Hours, curse lines like these have been left out, with Psalms 58, 83 and 109 (General Instruction 131). The Orthodox read the whole Psalter each week and keep it complete.
views.J: Jewish tradition prays it as David's and Israel's plea against persecutors. The Sabbath prayer Nishmat quotes 35:10, and later Jewish writers cited "every bone in me will say" to explain swaying in prayer.
views.X: John 15:25 applies 35:19 (or 69:4) to the hatred Jesus met. Augustine and others read the enemies as the persecutors of Christ and the church; many modern Christians pray the psalm for the falsely accused and the oppressed.

deep.h: How to pray a curse psalm
deep.b: Readers have taken four main roads. (1) Leave it out: some lectionaries and prayer books skip the curse lines. (2) Pray it against evil: the Orthodox and many medieval readers turned the enemies into demons, sins and passions. (3) Pray it in Christ: Bonhoeffer argued that the curse psalms are prayed through Christ, who bore God's judgment on sin and prayed for his enemies. (4) Pray it honestly: C. S. Lewis called the curses a natural result of injustice, worse in the hearts of those who caused it, and Erich Zenger argued that they hand vengeance to God and so break the cycle of violence. In this psalm, the speaker does no harm; he asks God to judge and promises to praise.

echoes: John 15:25; Psalm 69:4; Psalm 109:3; Psalm 40:14–15; Psalm 70:2–3; John 20:28; Romans 12:19; Deuteronomy 32:35; 1 Kings 8:31–32

settings.what: A plea of the falsely accused
settings.to: God as judge and warrior; the friends who will rejoice with him (35:27)
settings.when: after false witnesses have brought charges (35:11) and former friends have turned on him (35:12–16)
settings.why: to ask God to judge between him and his accusers, to give voice to the pain of betrayal, and to promise public praise when he is cleared
settings.readers: After the exile, Jewish communities facing hostile neighbors and slander (Nehemiah 4; Ezra 4) could pray it as Israel's own plea.
views: A man accused in a trial at the temple asks for God's verdict (Kraus).
The military language suggests a king betrayed by allies (Craigie).

traditions.q: Should the curse psalms be prayed in worship?
views: The Liturgy of the Hours leaves out Psalms 58, 83 and 109 and certain curse verses of other psalms, for pastoral reasons, while keeping them in Scripture (General Instruction of the Liturgy of the Hours 131).
The whole Psalter is read every week without omission; the curses are prayed against the demons and the passions, the soul's real enemies.
Bonhoeffer taught that the curse psalms are prayed through Christ, who bore God's vengeance on sin and prayed for his enemies; they are kept, not cut.
Churches that sing only psalms sing them whole; Calvin taught they may be prayed only against the enemies of God's kingdom, with pure zeal and not personal spite.
The 1662 Prayer Book reads the whole Psalter each month; many modern Anglican psalters mark the harshest verses as optional.

title: Rebellion's Oracle and the Spring of Life
sum: Psalm 36 (Greek 35) sets two pictures side by side. First, the wicked man: Rebellion speaks to him like a prophet, he has no dread of God, he flatters himself, and he lies awake plotting. Then, God: his loyal love fills the heavens, his righteousness is like the great mountains, and people take shelter under his wings, feast in his house and drink from his river of delights. "With you is the spring of life; in your light we see light."
The psalm ends with a short prayer to be kept from the proud, and a glimpse of the evildoers fallen. Paul quotes 36:1 in Romans 3:18.

views.H: The title calls David "the servant of the LORD", as in Psalm 18. Tradition has seen in the wicked man Saul or the enemies of David's court.
views.C: A mixed psalm: wisdom portrait (36:1–4), hymn (36:5–9) and lament (36:10–12). The temple imagery (wings, house, river) suggests a temple setting; some suggest an accused person seeking asylum in the sanctuary.
views.L: Christian morning prayer has long used 36:5–10 for its light imagery. 36:9 appears in hymns and as a university motto (Columbia, In lumine tuo videbimus lumen).
views.J: The Talmud (Hullin 5b) reads "humans and animals" (36:6) of people who are wise yet make themselves humble as animals before God.
views.X: Paul uses 36:1 in his chain of texts on universal sin (Romans 3:18). Christian writers read 36:9 of the Trinity and of Christ the light (John 1:4; 8:12).

echoes: Romans 3:18; Micah 2:1; Genesis 2:10; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Revelation 22:1–2; John 1:4; John 8:12; Ruth 2:12; Matthew 23:37

settings.what: A portrait of the wicked and a hymn to God's love
settings.by: the psalmist (the title: David, the servant of the LORD)
settings.to: the congregation (36:1–9, with "we" in 36:9) and God (36:5–12)
settings.when: temple worship; the speaker feels the wicked close by (36:11)
settings.why: to set the self-deceived life of the wicked against the abundant life found in God's presence, and so to strengthen those tempted by the wicked man's success
settings.readers: After the exile the temple feast and the river of delights became pictures of the life Israel hoped for in God's restored house.

title: The Humble Will Have the Land
sum: Psalm 37 (Greek 36) is an alphabet of wisdom sayings from an old man to the young. Its message: do not burn with envy when the wicked succeed. They will dry up like grass. Trust the LORD, do good, wait for him. The humble, the righteous, those who wait for God will take possession of the land, while the wicked will be cut off. The wicked borrow and do not repay; the righteous give.

It is closer to Proverbs than to prayer: God is spoken about, not to. Jesus' beatitude "Blessed are the gentle, because they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5) comes from 37:11, where the Greek uses the same word for "the humble". The community at Qumran wrote a commentary on it (4Q171), reading the wicked as their enemies.

views.H: "I was a young man, and now I am old too" (37:25) fits an aged David passing on what he learned. The title says only "Of David".
views.C: A wisdom acrostic, like Proverbs in form and theme, probably from after the exile when the land and its possession were burning questions. Its confident teaching on reward is balanced in the Psalter by Psalm 73 and by Job.
views.L: The psalm is used in Christian morning prayer and in times of injustice. Its verse 37:25 comes near the end of the Jewish grace after meals.
views.J: The Talmud (Berakhot 7b) discusses 37:1 against Proverbs 28:4: may one oppose the wicked? The Qumran pesher (4Q171) applied the psalm to the Teacher of Righteousness, the Wicked Priest and "the congregation of the poor".
views.X: Matthew 5:5 quotes 37:11. Christian readers ask whether "the land" means Israel's land, the whole earth, or the new creation.

deep.b: Most letters open a pair of verses: alef 1–2, bet 3–4, gimel 5–6, dalet 7, he 8–9, waw 10–11, zayin 12–13, chet 14–15, tet 16–17, yod 18–19, kaf 20, lamed 21–22, mem 23–24, nun 25–26, samekh 27–28a, ayin 28b–29 (the ayin line is missing in the Masoretic Text but preserved by a Qumran commentary and the Greek; see the variant at 37:28), pe 30–31, tsade 32–33, qof 34, resh 35–36, shin 37–38, tav 39–40.

4Q171 (4QpPs-a), copied about the turn of the era, is a pesher, a line-by-line commentary that reads the psalm as a prophecy of the writers' own time. It sees "the wicked" as the Wicked Priest and the men of violence, and "the humble who will take possession of the land" as "the congregation of the poor", who will survive the time of trial and inherit the earth. It is one of the oldest surviving commentaries on any psalm.

echoes: Matthew 5:5; Proverbs 24:19–20; Proverbs 15:16; Proverbs 16:3; Psalm 73:1–28; Psalm 1:1–6; Job 21:7–13; Deuteronomy 4:1; Isaiah 57:13

settings.what: An old teacher's alphabet of advice
settings.by: an elder sage (the title: David; 37:25 says he is old)
settings.to: a younger listener tempted to envy the wicked ("you", 37:1–8, 37:27, 37:34, 37:37)
settings.when: a time when the wicked prosper and the humble lose ground and land
settings.why: to cool anger and envy, to promise that God will set things right in time, and to shape the listener's habits: trust, generosity, patience
settings.readers: For Jews after the exile, with land held by others and debt common (Nehemiah 5), "take possession of the land" was a living hope.
views: A teacher instructs pupils, as in Proverbs.
The psalm was used to steady the poor faithful in a divided community (as at Qumran).

traditions.q: Who will "take possession of the land" (37:11; Matthew 5:5)?
views: Classic dispensationalists hold that the land promises belong to ethnic Israel and will be fulfilled literally in the future kingdom; Matthew 5:5 looks to that earthly reign.
Progressive dispensationalists (Blaising and Bock) agree that Israel's land promise stands, but hold that it is also widened into the renewed earth shared by all God's people.
In Christ the promise of the land grows into the promise of the whole renewed creation for all believers (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16).
The beatitude promises the kingdom of God, the new earth, received by the humble; the land of Israel was its sign (Catechism 1716).

title: No Healthy Spot
sum: Psalm 38 (Greek 37) is the prayer of a man very ill, who believes his sickness is God's discipline for his sin. He describes his body in detail: arrows in him, wounds that stink, burning sides, a throbbing heart, failing eyes. His friends stand back; his enemies set traps. He does not argue with them. He keeps silent like a deaf man, confesses his guilt, and asks God not to stay far away.
It is the third of the seven penitential psalms, and its title connects it to the "remembrance" offering. Luke seems to echo 38:11 at the cross.

views.H: Tradition sets it in David's later life, after his sin, when his counselors and family turned against him.
views.C: An individual lament of a sick person, with confession of sin. It has 22 verses like an alphabet poem, but is not an acrostic. It may have been used with the memorial offering (title) at the temple.
views.L: The third penitential psalm, used in Lent. The Greek title "concerning the Sabbath" suggests it was once sung on that day.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition links the psalm to David's illness and reads it as a model of confession. Rashi takes the title to mean a psalm for bringing one's trouble before God's remembrance.
views.X: Christian commentators heard Christ's passion in 38:11 and 38:13, and the voice of the sinner in the rest; Augustine reads it as the whole Christ, head and body.

echoes: Psalm 6:1; Luke 23:49; Isaiah 53:7; Isaiah 1:5–6; Job 19:13–19; Leviticus 2:2; Matthew 26:63

settings.what: A sick man's confession and plea
settings.when: in serious illness that the speaker takes as discipline for sin; friends have withdrawn and enemies plot
settings.why: to confess and to ask for healing and God's nearness, without self-defense before human accusers
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, who read their national suffering as discipline for sin (Ezra 9:6–7; Nehemiah 9:33), the psalm gave words for repentance and hope together.

title: A Puff of Air
sum: Psalm 39 (Greek 38) begins with a man who tried to keep quiet. He muzzled his mouth so as not to sin in front of the wicked, but the pain burned until he spoke. When he speaks, it is not to accuse others but to ask God to show him how short life is: a few handbreadths, a puff of air, a shadow rushing about. His only hope is God, so he asks for rescue from his sins and for God to look away so he can smile once more before he goes.

It is among the bleakest psalms, close to Job and Ecclesiastes, and it ends without the usual turn to praise. Brahms set part of it in his German Requiem, and the Book of Common Prayer used it at funerals.

views.H: The title names Jeduthun, one of David's chief musicians, perhaps as the singer it was given to.
views.C: An individual lament with strong wisdom elements, sharing vocabulary with Job (39:13; Job 7:19; 10:20) and Ecclesiastes (hevel). Many date it late.
views.L: Used at funerals and on the theme of mortality (with Psalm 90) in the Book of Common Prayer; set by Brahms (A German Requiem, movement 3).
views.J: Jewish tradition reads 39:12 with Leviticus 25:23: Israel lives as God's guests on his land. 39:5–6 appear in reflections on mortality.
views.X: Christian readers connect 39:12 with Hebrews 11:13 and 1 Peter 2:11 (believers as foreigners on earth) and read the psalm as an honest prayer before the hope of the resurrection.

echoes: Job 7:16; Job 7:19; Job 10:20; Ecclesiastes 1:2; Leviticus 25:23; 1 Chronicles 29:15; Genesis 23:4; Hebrews 11:13; 1 Peter 2:11; Psalm 90:12; James 4:14

settings.to: the listener, as the poet explains how his prayer came about
settings.when: while the wicked were near and the poet was suffering
settings.why: to show why he finally spoke: holding in the pain did no good
settings.readers: It gave the community words for the struggle to speak honestly to God without giving scoffers an opening.

settings.what: A prayer about the shortness of life
settings.when: under God's discipline (39:10–11), aware of death
settings.why: to ask God to teach him his limits, forgive him, and give him relief before death; the poet throws himself on God as a guest on God's land
settings.readers: For Israelites after the exile, who were again "foreigners and lodgers" in a land ruled by others, 39:12 had a sharp edge.

title: Ears You Have Dug
sum: Psalm 40 (Greek 39) begins with thanks. The poet waited and waited for the LORD, who lifted him out of a muddy pit and put a new song in his mouth. Then he says something surprising: God did not want sacrifices and offerings; God dug out ears for him, and he answered, "Look, I have come", with God's law deep inside him. He has told the good news in the great gathering. Then, suddenly, troubles and guilt close in again, and he prays urgently for help (40:11–17).
Hebrews 10:5–10 quotes 40:6–8 from the Greek, which reads "a body you prepared for me", and makes it Christ's word on coming into the world. The last section, 40:13–17, appears again as Psalm 70.
readings: Read as a thanksgiving and a lament

The psalm joins a thank-you song (40:1–10) and a cry for help (40:11–17). Whether they were joined by an editor or composed together, the order teaches something: past rescue gives courage when new trouble comes.

Hebrews hears the Son speaking (Hebrews 10:5–7): God does not want animal offerings but a body, a whole human life given in obedience. The offering of that body "once for all" ends the old sacrifices (Hebrews 10:10–14).

Jewish readers hear David, or any faithful Israelite, saying what the prophets said: God wants listening ears and a heart that holds his law (1 Samuel 15:22; Jeremiah 7:22–23). The psalm does not do away with the temple; it says what gives offerings their worth.

views.H: Readers who trust the title hear David after a rescue, perhaps as king ("the scroll of the book" as the king's copy of the law, Deuteronomy 17:18–19).
views.C: Most scholars see two parts: an individual thanksgiving (40:1–10) and a lament (40:11–17), the second also found as Psalm 70. Some think a king speaks, given the public setting and the book; others a worshiper bringing a written vow.
views.L: The Roman lectionary sets Psalm 40 with Hebrews 10:4–10 on the feast of the Annunciation (25 March), because of Hebrews 10:5 ("when he comes into the world"). The opening verses are set by Mendelssohn and sung by U2 ("40").
views.J: Medieval commentators such as Radak read 40:6 with Jeremiah 7:22–23: God's first demand was obedience, and offerings come after it. Rashi reads "the scroll of the book" as the Torah written for Israel.
views.X: Hebrews 10:5–10 is the key Christian reading. The church fathers saw the incarnation in "a body you prepared". Many modern Christian scholars hold that Hebrews reads the psalm's ideal of obedience as fulfilled in Christ, rather than claiming David foresaw it.

deep.h: Ears or a body: Psalm 40:6 and Hebrews 10:5
deep.b:
The Hebrew of 40:6 (Hebrew Bibles 40:7) says 'oznayim karita li, "ears you have dug for me". The oldest form of the Greek translation probably said the same: ōtia de katērtisō moi, "but ears you have prepared for me". Rahlfs prints this in his edition, supported by the Latin Psalter made from the Greek (aures). But the great Greek Bibles of the 300s and 400s (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus) read sōma, "a body", and so does Hebrews 10:5.

Three explanations are offered. A copying slip: Greek capitals written without spaces could turn ...ΗΘΕΛΗΣΑΣΩΤΙΑ into ...ΗΘΕΛΗΣΑΣΣΩΜΑ (the last letter of the verb doubled, TI read as M). A translator's paraphrase: the first translator, or an early reviser, put the whole body for the ears, since a body is what obeys. Hebrews' own wording: the author of Hebrews chose or shaped the reading, and later Christian copyists brought Greek Bibles into line with it (Jobes argues for deliberate shaping by Hebrews for sound and sense).

Whatever its origin, Hebrews uses the word with purpose: "we have been made holy, through the offering of Jesus Christ's body, once for all" (Hebrews 10:10). Hebrews also changes "you did not ask for" to "did not please you" and ends the quotation at "to do your will, O God", leaving out "is my delight" and "your law is in my very core". The Plain follows the Hebrew; the variant lets the reader see the Greek readings in place.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the ear and the body are one idea
deep.b: My suggestion is that the Hebrew already points toward the Greek. "Dug ears" is a picture of God making a person able to hear, and in Hebrew thought hearing means obeying (shama' is both). Verse 8 then moves from the ear to the whole inner body (me'ai, "my insides"), where the law now lives. A translator who rendered "ears" by "body" would be summing up the movement of 40:6–8 rather than inventing. This overlaps with the synecdoche view in commentaries (for example Lane and Attridge on Hebrews), but goes further in reading 40:8 as the bridge.

echoes: Hebrews 10:5–10; 1 Samuel 15:22; Hosea 6:6; Jeremiah 7:22–23; Isaiah 50:5; Jeremiah 31:33; Deuteronomy 17:18–19; Psalm 70:1–5; Psalm 51:16–17; Psalm 33:3

settings.to: the great gathering at the temple (40:9–10) and God (40:5–10)
settings.when: after a rescue from a deadly danger ("the pit", 40:2); probably at the temple, where thank offerings were brought
settings.why: to tell the story of rescue in public, so that "many will see" and trust, and to say what God really wants: an obedient life
settings.readers: After the exile, when sacrifice resumed in the rebuilt temple, the psalm reminded worshipers what gave offerings their meaning.
views: The scroll is the king's law (Deuteronomy 17:18–19), and the great gathering is the nation.
The scroll is a written vow or the Torah; any Israelite could pray it.

settings.when: troubles and sins have closed in again (40:12)
settings.why: to ask for quick help, shame for the mockers and joy for those who seek God
settings.readers: This section was also used alone as Psalm 70, a short prayer for urgent need.

traditions.q: Hebrews 10 (quoting Psalm 40:6–8) says Christ's body was offered once for all. Is the Lord's Supper a sacrifice?
views: The Mass makes present the one sacrifice of the cross, offered in an unbloody way; it is not a new or repeated sacrifice (Catechism 1366–1367; Trent, Session 22).
The Eucharist is the "bloodless sacrifice" in which Christ's one offering is present; Christ is both offerer and offered.
The Supper is Christ's gift of his true body and blood, not a sacrifice we offer to earn forgiveness; at most it is a sacrifice of thanks (Apology of the Augsburg Confession 24).
The Supper is not a sacrifice but a commemoration of Christ's one offering and a spiritual feeding on him (Westminster Confession 29.2).
The Thirty-Nine Articles reject the "sacrifices of Masses" as a repeated offering (Article 31); Anglo-Catholic Anglicans speak of the Eucharist as a pleading of the one sacrifice.

title: The Friend Who Ate My Bread
sum: Psalm 41 (Greek 40), the last psalm of Book I, begins like Psalm 1 with "Happy": happy the one who cares for the weak, for God will care for him when he is sick. Then the speaker tells his own story: he is sick, he has confessed his sin, and his enemies are waiting for him to die. Visitors gossip; even his closest friend, who ate at his table, has turned on him. He asks God to raise him up.
Jesus applies 41:9 to Judas (John 13:18). Verse 13 is not part of the psalm but the closing blessing of Book I of the Psalter, the first of four such doxologies.

views.H: Tradition connects the betraying friend with Ahithophel, David's counselor who joined Absalom (2 Samuel 15:12, 31), and the illness with David's last years.
views.C: A thanksgiving or lament of a sick person, framed by a wisdom saying (41:1–3). The closing doxology (41:13) was added when Book I was put together as a collection. Psalms 1 and 41 both begin with ashrei, framing the book.
views.L: The doxology (41:13) is used as a blessing in Jewish and Christian worship. Christian readers link the psalm with Holy Week and the betrayal of Judas.
views.J: The Talmud (Nedarim 40a) reads 41:1 as praise for visiting the sick. The Mishnah (Berakhot 9:5) says blessings in the temple once ended "forever", and the longer "from the ages past to the ages to come" was made the rule against those who denied a world to come.
views.X: John 13:18 quotes 41:9 at the Last Supper (compare Acts 1:16, where other psalms are applied to Judas). Christians read the psalm as both the sufferer's prayer and a picture of Christ betrayed by a friend.

deep.b: Book I of the Psalms (Psalms 1–41) is almost all "of David" (only 1, 2, 10 and 33 lack his name). It begins with "Happy" (1:1) and ends with "Happy" (41:1), and then a blessing: "Blessed be the LORD, the God of Israel, from the ages past to the ages to come. Amen and Amen." Similar blessings close Book II (72:18–19), Book III (89:52) and Book IV (106:48), and Psalm 150 closes Book V. Gerald Wilson and others argue that these markers show the Psalter was shaped as a book, to be read in order, not only sung psalm by psalm.

echoes: John 13:18; 2 Samuel 15:12; 2 Samuel 15:31; Psalm 55:12–14; Psalm 1:1; Psalm 72:18–19; Psalm 89:52; Psalm 106:48; 1 Chronicles 16:36

settings.what: A sick man's thanksgiving and complaint
settings.when: in sickness, surrounded by enemies hoping for his death and a friend who has betrayed him
settings.why: to say that God cares for those who care for the weak, and to plead for healing and vindication against a false friend
settings.readers: Israel after the exile, which had known betrayal and foreign rule, prayed it as the voice of the faithful sufferer, and read 41:1 as a call to care for the sick and poor.

settings.what: The closing blessing of Book I
settings.when: when the first collection of psalms was set in its place
settings.why: to close the first book with a blessing of God and the people's "Amen and Amen"
settings.readers: For readers of the finished Psalter, it marks the end of the first of five books, which Jewish tradition compares to the five books of Moses.
